items.headline: Machine learning methods move self-driving labs closer to materials discovery at scale
items.excerpt: Washington University researchers trained models on 4,000 metal-organic framework linker transformations so the system 'reads chemistry like a chemist,' surfacing 10 new viable water-harvesting materials without brute-force screening. A parallel polymer effort automates data curation from the literature to rank high-potential candidates.

items.headline: Could 12 inches of rain hit New York City? AI maps plausible rare storms
items.excerpt: MIT researchers built a machine-learning method called eta-learning that generates physically plausible extreme-weather scenarios without needing historical events of similar magnitude. It can map hypothetical 12-inch rainfalls over New York so planners can stress-test infrastructure against storms riskier than anything on record.

items.headline: Brain recordings hint at how AI reads facial expressions differently from us
items.excerpt: York University researchers compared human brain recordings, primate neurons and artificial neural networks on facial-expression processing, finding the networks hit high accuracy through fundamentally non-biological computations. The takeaway: getting the right answer is not the same as solving the problem in a brain-like way.

items.headline: Research shows AI can fast track mental health care
items.excerpt: Victoria University researchers ran one million Reddit threads through language models to infer the underlying causes behind mental-health disclosures. PaLM 2 matched human psychiatrist classifications in about 80% of cases, pointing to triage and screening uses.

items.headline: AI helps identify regulatory hub for aging in hematopoietic stem cells
items.excerpt: Tohoku University used AI analysis to pinpoint Pbx1 as a master regulator of aging in blood-forming stem cells. Raising Pbx1 in young stem cells reproduced aged-cell traits, including reduced mature blood-cell output and altered platelet production.

items.headline: Shared-memory AI system lets microscope components coordinate in real time
items.excerpt: Postdoc Arco Bast built a shared-memory architecture that lets separate microscope components read common state, collapsing experiment setup from months to days. With Anthropic he released a Model Hardware Standard so AI agents can observe and adjust instruments live.

items.headline: DigBat: An AI-ready digital platform for solid-state battery research
items.excerpt: Tohoku University's DigBat consolidates experimental and computational solid-electrolyte data with machine-learning tooling and an AI assistant. As of June 2026 it holds 3,816 experimental electrolytes and 27,645 conductivity entries for training predictive models.

items.headline: Does Computer Science Need Computers?
items.excerpt: Quanta examines how much of computer science is really about machines, and how many of its central questions would never have been asked without them. The piece reframes theory and experiment in a field now dominated by empirical AI results.

items.headline: When AI designs a drug, who gets the credit?
items.excerpt: US courts have held that only humans can be named inventors, so AI-designed drugs are filed under human names - Insilico listed five people on a molecule its models generated. Lawyers warn that wrong-inventor claims could become a route to invalidating AI-derived patents.

items.headline: AI models flub these intelligence tests. Can you fare any better?
items.excerpt: Seven puzzles and games expose where frontier models' reasoning breaks down, and readers can try the same tests themselves. The exercise doubles as an argument about what current AI benchmarks fail to capture.

items.headline: FAU Researchers Use Quantum Machine Learning to Predict Heart Disease
items.excerpt: Florida Atlantic University researchers report a quantum machine learning model that reached 90.26% accuracy predicting heart disease across 918 patient records. It is one of the clearer near-term tests of whether QML gives any edge on real clinical tabular data.

items.headline: Researchers Use IBM Quantum Computer to Test Drug-Docking Method
items.excerpt: A team demonstrated a resource-efficient hybrid quantum-classical molecular docking method on an IBM quantum processor. The run is a concrete probe of where quantum hardware could slot into structure-based drug discovery pipelines.

items.headline: GlucoFM: Foundation model for continuous glucose monitoring
items.excerpt: Google Research introduces GlucoFM, a foundation model trained on continuous glucose monitor streams for forecasting and downstream metabolic tasks. It extends the sensor-foundation-model line from wearables into a dense clinical time-series domain.

items.headline: An AI tool for prioritizing candidate biomarkers from wearable sensor data
items.excerpt: Google Research describes a system that mines wearable sensor streams to rank candidate digital biomarkers for follow-up study. The aim is to cut the manual hypothesis-triage step that slows down sensor-based health research.

items.headline: What's in Merck and Moderna's cancer vaccine algorithm?
items.excerpt: STAT digs into the neoantigen-selection algorithm behind Merck and Moderna's individualized cancer vaccine, the model that decides which mutations each patient's shot targets. The details matter because the algorithm, not the chemistry, is the hard-to-copy asset.

items.headline: The Way You Draw Can Reveal Parkinson's Disease With Up to 99% Accuracy, Study Reveals
items.excerpt: A machine-learning analysis of drawing and handwriting dynamics separated Parkinson's patients from controls with up to 99% accuracy. The signal sits in stroke timing and pressure rather than the finished image, making cheap tablet-based screening plausible.

items.headline: New kind of AI uses a fresh approach to reasoning - researchers say it costs up to 11 times less to run
items.excerpt: Researchers describe a vector-based approach to cognition that they say reasons at up to 11 times lower inference cost than a leading OpenAI model. If it holds, cheap reasoning changes what kinds of scientific workloads can be run at scale.

items.headline: AI Identifies Pre-existing Antimicrobial Antibody Profile That May Predict Immune Response to Vaccination
items.excerpt: Machine learning on sentinel antibody profiles picked out a pre-existing antimicrobial signature that predicts how strongly a person responds to vaccination. The profiling could guide vaccine design, trial enrollment and care for people at risk of weak responses.
